title: Reading the Great Books in the Age of AI
author: Devin Stauffer
summary: Devin Stauffer, a University of Texas government professor, argues that the Great Books are more precious in the age of AI, both for the habits of mind they build and for the questions they raise. He says reading them is counter-cultural in an age of maximum information and minimum reflection, and that slow, active reading is an antidote to what Solzhenitsyn called hastiness and superficiality. Using Machiavelli's letter about entering the ancient courts of ancient men each evening, he shows what undistracted reading can be. He then argues the books deal with rich versions of simple questions and that AI revives the old question of what it means to be human. He stages a contrast between Aristotle, who would fear AI taking thinking and judging from us, and Hobbes, who would welcome it as another tool of power over nature. He concludes that a machine cannot settle this debate because it lacks human experience, so readers should read the authors themselves instead of summaries.
points: Reading the Great Books requires slowing down, which makes it a deliberate counterweight to screens and algorithmic distraction.
The Great Books pose simple, childlike questions about justice, virtue and happiness, and give rich, competing answers rather than a single verdict.
AI forces an old question back into view: what is distinctive about thinking as a human being?
Aristotle and Hobbes offer opposing views of human nature, and so of whether AI threatens or expresses our humanity.
Because machines cannot draw on lived experience of anger, hope or longing, readers must consult the primary texts themselves instead of summaries.
quotes: We live in an age of maximum information but minimum reflection.

There is perhaps no greater antidote to hastiness and superficiality than reading the Great Books, which can’t be read well without slowing down, taking one’s time, and reflecting as deeply as one can on complex arguments and profound reflections.
One of the things that makes the Great Books great is that they contain very rich and very complex treatments of very simple questions.
One of the new questions AI is forcing us to confront is in fact an old question: What does it mean to be human?
so too human beings sitting on couches scrolling through social media feeds while AI does the work of thinking and judging for them are not living fully human lives.
The authors of the Great Books rarely agree with each other. That is one of the virtues of reading them, because it compels one to become a participant in a vast debate.
To think well about who is right between Aristotle and Hobbes, one should read their books—not my summaries or AI’s—ponder their arguments, and avoid rushing to conclusions
